newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Re-election, reform top Brazil's Congress agenda.
newsitem.headline: Re-election, reform top Brazil's Congress agenda.

text.p: Activity in Brazil's Congress this week is likely to focus on the government's attempts to get its re-election drive under way and on the voting of proposed alterations to its civil service reform.

Government leaders have said they expect a special committee to begin debating on Wednesday a proposed constitutional amendment that would allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso the chance of a second term.

But the Brazilian Progressive Party (PPB), one of the four biggest in the lower house, insists it must wait for authorization from party delegates before naming its members to the committee, a process expected to take until the weekend.

Observers say the PPB is playing for time because it does not want to be associated with the government's re-election plans in the run-up to the second and final vote in Sao Paulo's municipal elections where its candidate is leading polls.
The PPB is also the party of Paulo Maluf, the outgoing Sao Paulo mayor who has said he may run for president in 1998.

Newspapers reported the PPB, with its eye on the November 15 election in Sao Paulo, might also object to some of the key points of the government's civil service reform which was approved in principle last week in a lower house committee.
The committee is due to begin voting on a series of proposed alterations to the bill on Tuesday.

Gazeta Mercatil said the PPB would suggest scrapping a clause that would allow state and municipal governments that spend more than 60 percent of receipts on pay to dismiss currently unsackable workers.
But, the newspaper said, the PPB would probably take a more pro-reform approach once the Sao Paulo election was over.
Two other important reforms -- of the pension and tax systems -- were unlikely to advance this week.
The pension reform is awaiting nomination of a senator to guide it through the upper house where the government will seek to restore key points defeated in the Chamber of Deputies.

A first meeting of a lower house committee to debate the tax reform was scheduled for Wednesday, but officials doubted quorum would be reached as many deputies remain away from Brasilia campaigning for November's elections.
The Senate may vote this week on a bill outlining the small print of a new financial transaction tax which would help fund the health service.
